hints: Focus on this as a competition between halogens, where only the stronger oxidising agent can displace the other from solution.
Remember the reactivity order down Group 17 is chlorine > bromine > iodine, so bromine is a stronger oxidiser than iodine.
Ask yourself if iodine is powerful enough to remove electrons from bromide ions to form bromine, and see what that tells you about reaction.
walkthrough:
**Recall the halogen displacement rule**

Think of halogens competing for electrons. A more reactive halogen will oxidise the halide ion of a less reactive halogen.

Reactivity trend:
$$\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$$

**Work out what would have to happen**

For a reaction, iodine would need to oxidise bromide to bromine, while iodine itself is reduced to iodide.

Hypothetical equation if it reacted:
$$\text{I}_2 + 2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + 2\text{I}^-$$

**Check oxidising strength**

Bromine is above iodine in Group 17, so $\text{Br}_2$ is a stronger oxidising agent than $\text{I}_2$. That means $\text{Br}^-$ is more stable and holds its electrons more tightly than $\text{I}^-$ does.

So $\text{I}_2$ is too weak to take electrons from $\text{Br}^-$.

**Conclude the observation**

Since iodine cannot oxidise bromide ions, no displacement happens. The solution just contains $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{NaBr}$ mixed together with no change in oxidation state.

options.A: Incorrect. There is no reaction at all, so we cannot describe it as a reaction without oxidation state changes. This option may tempt students who think mixing always causes some physical change.
options.B: Incorrect. This describes $\text{I}_2 + 2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + 2\text{I}^-$, where bromide is oxidised from -1 to 0 and iodine is reduced from 0 to -1. This is backwards because iodine is a weaker oxidiser than bromine and cannot oxidise bromide.
options.C: Incorrect. Bromide ions ($\text{Br}^-$) are already at oxidation state -1 and cannot easily be reduced further, while iodine atoms in $\text{I}_2$ at 0 cannot be oxidised by bromide. This reverses the correct ideas of oxidation and reduction.
options.D: Correct. Iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot displace bromine from sodium bromide. No electron transfer occurs and oxidation states stay as $\text{I}_2$ (0) and $\text{Br}^-$ (-1).
